title: Thyroid Disorders: Hyperthyroidism, Hypothyroidism & Emergency Nursing Care
html:
Thyroid hormone affects heart rate, temperature, energy use, bowel activity, and cognition. Adult nursing care starts with the whole client—not a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) value alone. Hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism may develop gradually, while thyroid storm and severe decompensated hypothyroidism are emergencies. Treatment decisions depend on the cause, comorbidities, current medications, pregnancy status, and authorized orders.

Learning goals

  • Compare common hyperthyroid and hypothyroid cues with thyroid test patterns.
  • Recognize thyroid storm and severe decompensated hypothyroidism early.
  • Monitor antithyroid therapy, thyroid-hormone replacement, and definitive treatments safely.
  • Prioritize airway, bleeding, and hypocalcemia assessment after thyroidectomy.
  • Use teach-back to support follow-up and prevent avoidable deterioration.

Read the pattern, then the person

In primary hyperthyroidism, TSH is usually suppressed and free T4 and/or T3 are elevated; in primary hypothyroidism, TSH is usually high and free T4 low. These are patterns, not stand-alone diagnoses. Pituitary disease, acute illness, medications, pregnancy, and treatment status can alter interpretation. Review the trend and the laboratory reference range; ask about biotin or other supplements that may interfere with testing. Assess heart rate and rhythm, blood pressure, temperature, weight trend, hydration, sleep, bowel pattern, activity tolerance, skin, mental status, and neck or eye findings. Escalate a rapidly changing clinical picture even if a laboratory result is pending.

Hyperthyroidism: protect the heart and reduce strain

Excess hormone commonly causes heat intolerance, sweating, tremor, anxiety, insomnia, weight loss despite appetite, frequent stools, palpitations, tachycardia, and sometimes atrial fibrillation or heart failure. Graves disease may add goiter and thyroid eye disease; thyroiditis or autonomous nodules have different treatment implications. Check for chest pain, dyspnea, irregular pulse, dehydration, and impaired ability to eat or sleep. Offer a calm environment, rest, hydration and nutrition support as appropriate, and fall precautions if weak or dizzy.

Prescribed beta-blockers can relieve adrenergic symptoms but require pulse, blood-pressure, breathing, and perfusion reassessment; they do not correct hormone overproduction. Methimazole and propylthiouracil (PTU) inhibit thyroid-hormone synthesis. Methimazole is commonly used, but drug choice differs in specific situations such as early pregnancy and thyroid storm. Confirm orders and avoid substituting one drug for another. Teach the client taking an antithyroid drug to seek prompt evaluation for fever, sore throat, or other infection symptoms because rare agranulocytosis can develop abruptly; new jaundice, dark urine, severe abdominal pain, or marked fatigue also warrants urgent assessment for possible liver injury. Follow the prescribing clinician's instructions about holding medicine and obtaining a blood count; do not simply reassure or wait for the next routine appointment.

Thyroid storm: a clinical emergency

Thyroid storm is severe thyrotoxicosis with systemic decompensation. Watch for high fever, marked tachycardia or dysrhythmia, agitation or confusion, vomiting or diarrhea, dehydration, heart failure, hypotension, or shock—often after infection, surgery, medication interruption, or another major stressor. It is a clinical emergency; a single TSH or T4 value does not measure its severity. Activate the emergency response, assess airway and perfusion, obtain continuous cardiac and temperature monitoring, support ordered fluids and cooling, and help identify the trigger. In a monitored protocol, treatment may combine a beta-blocker when hemodynamically appropriate, an antithyroid drug, glucocorticoids, and iodine given only after the antithyroid drug so iodine is not used as substrate for new hormone synthesis. Medication order and timing belong to the authorized team; avoid independently giving iodine or aggressively lowering heart rate in a client with shock or decompensated heart failure.

Hypothyroidism: replacement and practical adherence

Low thyroid hormone may cause fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, weight gain, slowed thinking, depressed mood, bradycardia, and reduced exercise tolerance. Symptoms are nonspecific; assess anemia, medication effects, depression, and other causes as well. Levothyroxine replaces T4 and is usually a long-term treatment. Teach consistent daily administration as directed, typically on an empty stomach with water and a wait before breakfast; calcium, iron, some antacids, and food can reduce absorption, so the regimen should separate interfering products according to the clinician or pharmacist's instructions. Do not double or stop doses without guidance. Follow-up TSH and free T4 interpretation depends on whether disease is primary or central and on the timing of dose changes. In older adults or clients with coronary disease, monitor for chest pain, palpitations, or excess-replacement symptoms and follow cautious prescribed titration.

Severe decompensated hypothyroidism: do not wait for coma

Myxedema coma is a traditional name for life-threatening severe hypothyroidism; the person may be lethargic or confused rather than literally comatose. Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, low blood pressure, and altered mental status are danger cues, often with infection, cold exposure, sedatives, or other stress. Immediately escalate and protect airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, temperature, and cardiac status. Obtain ordered studies and support monitored thyroid-hormone and glucocorticoid treatment under the emergency plan. Handle warming and fluids carefully; avoid assuming the client is merely tired, depressed, or aging. Clinical stabilization and treatment of the precipitating illness are essential.

Definitive therapy and thyroidectomy safety

For selected causes of hyperthyroidism, the team may choose radioactive iodine or surgery; radioactive iodine is not appropriate during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and individualized precautions follow the treating service. After total thyroidectomy, the client generally needs thyroid-hormone replacement. Immediately after thyroid surgery, place airway and bleeding surveillance ahead of routine teaching. Watch for increasing neck swelling or tightness, stridor, difficulty breathing or swallowing, frequent swallowing, respiratory distress, or rapidly expanding drainage; activate the emergency pathway for suspected hematoma or airway compromise. Assess voice changes and follow prescribed calcium monitoring. Perioral or fingertip tingling, muscle cramps, spasms, or tetany can signal hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury and need prompt evaluation. Support the head and neck, monitor the incision, and ensure emergency airway equipment is available according to local policy.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Compare temperature, heart rate and rhythm, perfusion, mentation, breathing, bowel pattern, weight, medication history, and thyroid-test trends.
  2. Analyze cues: Decide whether symptoms fit overproduction, underproduction, a medication complication, a postoperative complication, or another illness.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway compromise after thyroidectomy, thyroid storm with organ dysfunction, severe decompensated hypothyroidism, dysrhythmia, and drug toxicity outrank routine education.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan monitored stabilization, order verification, trigger assessment, symptom support, and follow-up teaching with the multidisciplinary team.
  5. Take action: Escalate emergency cues, trend vital signs and rhythm, follow authorized medication sequencing, and report fever or sore throat during antithyroid therapy.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess airway, perfusion, temperature, rhythm, cognition, symptoms, treatment tolerance, laboratory trends, and ability to explain the home plan.

Clinical example

Two hours after thyroidectomy, a client becomes restless, repeatedly swallows, and says the neck feels tight. The RN immediately assesses breathing, voice, oxygenation, incision and neck swelling, calls for urgent help, and prepares for airway intervention under the local emergency plan. A normal-looking external dressing does not rule out a compressive neck hematoma. After the airway threat is addressed, the RN continues monitoring for hypocalcemia and confirms the replacement and follow-up plan.

Original educational synthesis. Thyroid testing, antithyroid drugs, hormone replacement, emergency treatment, and postoperative care require current client data, authorized orders, local protocols, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, certification, continuing education, or an official American Thyroid Association product.
